title: NEB Class 11 Chemistry — Bio-inorganic Chemistry — 2024
subject: chemistry
source: NEB Grade 11 Model Questions / NEB Past Papers 2020-2024

questions.question: Discuss the biological roles of sodium, potassium, calcium, and magnesium in the human body.
questions.solution:
**Na⁺/K⁺:** the membrane pump duo — nerve impulses and fluid balance. **Ca²⁺:** bones/teeth, blood clotting, muscle contraction. **Mg²⁺:** chlorophyll's centre and cofactor for ATP enzymes.

Deficiency shows fast: cramps (Ca/Mg), irregular heartbeat (K).
questions.knowledgeNote: Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase moves 3 Na⁺ out per 2 K⁺ in — the charge gradient behind every nerve signal.
questions.answer: **Sodium (Na⁺) and potassium (K⁺):** the principal extracellular and intracellular cations — they regulate **osmotic balance and water distribution**, maintain the body's acid–base (pH) balance, and generate the **nerve-impulse membrane potential** (the Na⁺/K⁺ pump) that underlies every nerve signal and muscle contraction. **Calcium:** ~99% of the body's calcium is in **bones and teeth** (as hydroxyapatite); ionic Ca²⁺ triggers **muscle contraction, blood clotting** and neurotransmitter release, and is essential to cell signalling. **Magnesium:** the **central atom of chlorophyll** (in plants), and in humans a cofactor of **over 300 enzymes** — including all ATP-using reactions — supporting nerve and muscle function and protein synthesis. **Deep point:** the four metals split the body's work by mobility and binding — Na⁺/K⁺ in solution doing fast signalling, Ca²⁺ switching between crystal and signal, Mg²⁺ locked into enzyme and pigment centres.

questions.question: Why is iron present in haemoglobin and magnesium in chlorophyll? What happens on deficiency?
questions.solution:
**Fe²⁺** in haem reversibly binds O₂ — oxygen transport. Deficiency → **anaemia** (low haemoglobin, fatigue).

**Mg²⁺** sits at chlorophyll's porphyrin centre, capturing light. Deficiency → **chlorosis** (yellowing leaves, failed photosynthesis).
questions.knowledgeNote: Haem and chlorophyll share the porphyrin ring — nature reuses one scaffold with different metal centres.
questions.answer: **Iron in haemoglobin:** Fe²⁺ sits at the centre of each haem porphyrin ring, where its open coordination site binds **O₂ reversibly** — the chemistry of oxygen transport. **Magnesium in chlorophyll:** Mg²⁺ sits at the centre of the porphyrin ring, where its electron configuration enables the **light absorption and electron transfer** of photosynthesis. **Deficiency of iron:** haemoglobin cannot be completed ⟹ **iron-deficiency anaemia** — pale, small red cells, fatigue and breathlessness from oxygen starvation. **Deficiency of magnesium:** chlorophyll cannot form ⟹ **chlorosis** (yellow leaves), collapsing photosynthesis and growth. **Deep point:** the two metals are biological counterparts — both porphyrin-centre ions, one moving O₂ through animals, the other harvesting light in plants; each deficiency starves its organism of its energy source.

questions.question: What is the role of iodine in the human body? What disorder does its deficiency cause?
questions.solution:
Iodine builds the thyroid hormones T₃/T₄, which set metabolic rate and drive brain development.

Deficiency → **goitre** (enlarged thyroid) and, in pregnancy/childhood, cretinism (stunted growth, impaired intellect) — prevented by iodised salt.
questions.knowledgeNote: The Himalayan belt's historic goitre problem is why Nepal iodises all edible salt by law.
questions.answer: **Role of iodine:** iodine is selectively taken up by the **thyroid gland** and used to synthesise the thyroid hormones **thyroxine (T₄) and triiodothyronine (T₃)**, which regulate the body's **basal metabolic rate**, growth and mental development. **Deficiency disorder:** **goitre** — the thyroid enlarges (visible swelling at the neck) as it strains to produce hormone without iodine; in children severe deficiency causes **cretinism** (stunted growth, mental retardation). Prevention is iodised salt. **Deep point:** iodine is the only element with a single-organ monopoly — the thyroid takes it up against a 30-fold gradient, which is why a pinch of iodised salt reaches one specific gland.

questions.question: What are metalloenzymes? Explain with the example of carbonic anhydrase.
questions.solution:
**Metalloenzymes** need a bound metal ion for catalysis.

**Carbonic anhydrase** holds Zn²⁺, which polarises water to generate OH⁻ that attacks CO₂: CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ — running ~10⁶ turnovers/second, clearing CO₂ from blood to lungs.
questions.knowledgeNote: Removing the metal kills the enzyme — the classic test that a protein is a metalloenzyme.
questions.answer: **Metalloenzymes:** enzymes that contain a **metal ion at (or near) the active site as an essential part of the catalyst** — the metal binds substrates, activates water, or shuttles electrons; remove the metal and the enzyme is inactive. **Carbonic anhydrase** is the classic example: a **zinc (Zn²⁺) metalloenzyme** in red cells that catalyses CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ (then HCO₃⁻ + H⁺) — the reaction that lets blood carry CO₂ as bicarbonate. **Mechanism:** Zn²⁺ at the active site binds and polarises a water molecule (lowering its pKa enormously), generating a bound **OH⁻** that attacks CO₂ thousands of times per second — the zinc is doing to water what an acid does, by coordination. **Deep point:** the metal ion is the enzyme's chemical hand — carbonic anhydrase's Zn²⁺ turns a reaction that takes seconds uncatalysed into one that runs ~10⁶ times per second, which is why you can breathe.

questions.question: Write the harmful effects of lead and mercury on human health.
questions.solution:
**Lead:** mimics calcium — damages developing brains (lower IQ), kidneys, and red-cell synthesis; sources include old paint and batteries.

**Mercury:** attacks the nervous system (tremors, Minamata disease); methylmercury bioaccumulates up food chains into fish.
questions.knowledgeNote: Both are cumulative poisons with no safe threshold in children — chelation therapy is the clinical response.
questions.answer: **Lead (Pb):** accumulates in bone and soft tissue; damages the **nervous system** (neurotoxic — learning impairment, especially in children), causes **anaemia** (blocks haem synthesis enzymes), kidney damage and elevated blood pressure; sources include leaded paint, batteries, contaminated water pipes. **Mercury (Hg):** organic **methylmercury** bioaccumulates in the food chain and attacks the **central nervous system** (tremor, memory loss, numbness) — the classic **Minamata disease** came from mercury-contaminated fish; inorganic mercury vapour damages kidneys and lungs; prenatal exposure severely harms fetal brain development. **Deep point:** both are cumulative poisons — the dose that matters is the lifetime body burden, which is why their regulation is set on chronic exposure, not acute symptoms.

questions.question: What is the role of cobalt in the human body? Name its vitamin.
questions.solution:
Cobalt is the metal centre of **vitamin B₁₂ (cobalamin)**, essential for red-cell formation and nerve myelination.

Deficiency → pernicious anaemia — historically treated with liver, now with B₁₂ supplements.
questions.knowledgeNote: B₁₂ is the only vitamin with a metal atom — and the only one plants cannot make, hence vegan supplementation.
questions.answer: **Role of cobalt:** cobalt is the central metal of **vitamin B₁₂ (cyanocobalamin)** — the only vitamin containing a metal. It is essential for **red blood cell formation**, DNA synthesis and the health of the myelin nerve sheath; cobalt deficiency (as B₁₂ deficiency) causes **pernicious anaemia**. **Its vitamin: vitamin B₁₂** (cobalamin). **Deep point:** cobalt's entire biological identity is that one coordination complex — the body needs it in micrograms, but without it the blood-making machinery stops.
